net orders: Orders received minus cancellations over a period. The cleanest measure of real demand for an aircraft maker.
A320neo: Airbus's best-selling single-aisle jet family. 'neo' = new engine option, roughly 15-20% less fuel burn than the original A320.
narrowbody: A single-aisle airliner (e.g. A320, 737) used mostly on short and medium routes.
widebody: A twin-aisle airliner (e.g. A350, 787) used mostly on long-haul routes.
MRO: Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul: the business of keeping aircraft and engines airworthy. A large, steady aftermarket revenue pool.
aftermarket: Revenue earned after a product is sold: spare parts, repairs and services. For engine makers it is often more profitable than selling the engine.
OEM: Original Equipment Manufacturer: the company that designs and builds the product (Airbus, Boeing, GE, Rolls-Royce), as opposed to third-party suppliers.
turbofan: The jet engine type on almost every airliner: a large front fan pushes most air around the core, which makes it quieter and more fuel efficient.
certification: Regulator approval (FAA, EASA, Rosaviatsia...) proving an aircraft type is safe. Requires hundreds of test flights; delays here delay deliveries.
air taxi: A small, usually electric aircraft (eVTOL) meant to carry a few passengers across a city, taking off and landing vertically.
eVTOL: electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing aircraft, the technology behind most planned air taxis.
trade secret: Confidential business information (designs, processes) protected by law. Misusing a rival's trade secrets can lead to large damages.
Series D: A fourth major round of venture funding. By this stage investors expect a clear path to revenue; failing to close one can threaten the company.
hydrogen-electric: A powertrain where hydrogen feeds a fuel cell that makes electricity for electric motors, emitting only water.
slots: Permission to take off or land at a congested airport at a specific time. At airports like LaGuardia they are scarce and very valuable.
antitrust: Competition law. Regulators review deals to make sure they do not give one company too much market power.
lessor: A company that owns aircraft and rents them to airlines. Lessors own around half of the world's airliner fleet.
damp-lease: Leasing an aircraft with part of the crew (usually pilots) included; between a dry lease (aircraft only) and a wet lease (aircraft, crew, maintenance, insurance).
profit outlook: Also called guidance: the earnings range a company tells investors to expect. Cutting it usually moves the share price.
jet fuel: Kerosene-based fuel. Typically 25-30% of an airline's costs, so oil price shocks hit airline profits quickly.
Federal Reserve: The US central bank. It sets interest rates to manage inflation and employment; its independence from the president is a long-standing norm.
net zero: Cutting greenhouse-gas emissions as far as possible and balancing the rest with removals, so the total added to the atmosphere is zero.
COP17: The 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, where governments negotiate nature-protection targets.
desalination: Removing salt from seawater or brackish water to make drinking water. Reliable but energy-hungry and expensive to build.
lithium: The key metal in rechargeable batteries for EVs and electronics. Extracting it often uses large amounts of water.
CBO: Congressional Budget Office: a non-partisan US agency that estimates the costs of policies for Congress.
deepfake: AI-generated video, image or audio that convincingly imitates a real person.
peer review: Checking of a scientific paper by independent experts before publication; the main quality filter in science.
robotaxi: A driverless taxi service (e.g. Waymo, Tesla), operating without a human safety driver.
green card: US lawful permanent residency, allowing someone to live and work in the US indefinitely.
visa programme: Here, a US work-visa scheme that lets employers hire foreign skilled workers.
Starlink: SpaceX's satellite internet network, now also sold to airlines for in-flight wi-fi.
spectrum: Radio frequencies governments license to telecom and satellite operators.
impairment: A write-down: the company admits an asset is worth less than it paid, and books the difference as a loss.
OPT: Optional Practical Training: lets international students work in the US for one to three years after graduating.
H-1B: The main US visa for skilled foreign workers, mostly used by tech companies.
CADE: Brazil's competition regulator, which reviews mergers and stakes for antitrust risk.
Chapter 11: US bankruptcy process that lets a company keep operating while it restructures its debts.
earnings per share: Profit divided by the number of shares. The headline number investors use to judge a company's results.
New Keynesian: The mainstream economic model behind modern central banking: prices adjust slowly, so interest rates and expectations can steady the economy.
monetary policy: What a central bank does with interest rates and money supply to control inflation and support jobs.
G7: Group of Seven large advanced economies: US, Japan, Germany, UK, France, Italy, Canada.
IMF: International Monetary Fund: lends to countries in trouble and publishes widely watched economic forecasts.
MQ-9 Reaper: A large US military drone used for surveillance and strikes.
Kunming-Montreal: The 2022 global biodiversity agreement with 23 targets for 2030, including protecting 30% of land and sea.
acre-feet: A US water unit: enough to cover one acre one foot deep, about 1.23 million litres.
pneumonic plague: The lung form of plague. It can spread person to person, but is treatable with antibiotics if caught early.
preprint: A research paper shared publicly before peer review.
NHTSA: The US road safety regulator, which collects crash data on self-driving cars.
Sentencing Commission: A US agency that writes the guidelines federal judges use to set prison sentences.
deference: When courts accept a government agency's interpretation of an unclear rule instead of deciding it themselves.
Strait of Hormuz: The narrow sea lane out of the Persian Gulf; about a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through it.
transition businesses: An energy company's low-carbon divisions: renewables, hydrogen, EV charging and similar.
Treasury yield: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow. When it rises, mortgages and company loans get more expensive too.
Brent: The main global benchmark price for crude oil.
earnings season: The few weeks each quarter when most big companies report their results.
correction: A fall of 10% or more in a stock index from its recent peak.
sanctions: Official restrictions or penalties imposed on a country to influence its behavior or policy.
bipartisan: Involving the agreement or cooperation of two political parties that usually oppose each other.
money-laundering: The illegal process of concealing the origins of money obtained illegally by passing it through a complex sequence of banking transfers or commercial transactions.
economic shocks: Unpredictable events that cause significant fluctuations in an economy's performance, such as sudden changes in supply or demand.
policymakers: Individuals or government bodies responsible for creating and implementing economic strategies to influence national or global financial conditions.
OpenAI: An artificial intelligence research laboratory focused on developing and deploying advanced AI technologies.
recording device: An electronic instrument designed to capture and store audio or visual information from its surroundings.
Houthi militia: A militant group based in Yemen currently engaged in a conflict with Saudi Arabia.
drone: An uncrewed aerial vehicle used here as a weapon for conducting strikes.
Nord Stream: A series of offshore natural gas pipelines in Europe that run under the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany.
sabotage: The deliberate act of damaging, destroying, or obstructing infrastructure, often for political or military advantage.
state of emergency: A government declaration that allows for the suspension of normal constitutional procedures and the granting of extraordinary powers to authorities.
PTI: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, a political party founded by Imran Khan that has held power in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province for over a decade.
provincial government: The administrative body responsible for the governance of a specific province within Pakistan's federal system.
military establishment: Refers to the powerful armed forces of Pakistan, which analysts argue exert significant influence over the country's political decision-making.
profit: The financial gain remaining after all expenses, debts, and operating costs have been subtracted from total revenue.
share: A unit of ownership interest in a corporation or financial asset that provides for an equal distribution of any profits declared.
Airbus A330neo: A wide-body jet aircraft manufactured by Airbus, used here as the specific model involved in the security incident.
Ben Gurion Airport: The primary international airport serving Tel Aviv, Israel, where the security inspection took place.
Transponder codes: Electronic signals transmitted by an aircraft to communicate its status, including emergency codes used to indicate unlawful interference.
Chapter 11 bankruptcy: A legal process that allows a company to reorganize its debts and assets while continuing to operate under court supervision.
franchisor: The entity that grants a license to a third party to conduct business under its brand and system.
corporate guarantees: A legal promise by a parent company to fulfill the financial obligations of its franchisees, such as lease payments, if the franchisee defaults.
unsecured claims: Debts or obligations that are not backed by any collateral or assets, placing the creditor in a lower priority for repayment during bankruptcy.
AI agents: Software programs capable of performing tasks or making decisions autonomously, which Smith warns could potentially 'break loose' or escape human control.
kill switches: Emergency mechanisms designed to immediately pause or shut down AI systems if they begin to operate in an uncontrolled or dangerous manner.
incident reports: Formal documentation that companies would be legally required to file to notify victims and authorities if their AI technology causes harm or security breaches.
self-regulatory regime: A system where an industry governs its own conduct and safety standards rather than adhering to legally mandated government oversight.
diesel: A type of fuel used primarily in heavy-duty engines and transportation vehicles.
legality: The state or quality of being in accordance with the law.
Falcon 9: A two-stage rocket designed and manufactured by SpaceX for the reliable and safe transport of satellites and the Dragon spacecraft into orbit.
Jellyfish effect: A visual phenomenon caused by rocket exhaust gases expanding in the upper atmosphere, often illuminated by sunlight during twilight or dawn.
7700 emergency code: A transponder code used by pilots to indicate an in-flight emergency, such as mechanical or technical problems.
Airbus A321: A narrow-body jet airliner manufactured by Airbus, used for short to medium-haul commercial flights.
squawked: The act of a pilot setting the aircraft's transponder to a specific four-digit code to communicate status to air traffic control.
normalize rates: The process of adjusting interest rates back toward a neutral level after a period of stimulus or emergency monetary policy.
central bank: The national financial institution responsible for overseeing a country's monetary system, currency, and interest rate policy.
resilient: The ability of an economy to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions or external shocks.
IPO: An initial public offering is the process by which a private company offers shares to the public in a new stock issuance for the first time.
AI: Artificial intelligence refers to computer systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as decision-making or data analysis.
Regulators: These are government or independent agencies responsible for exercising autonomous authority over an area of human activity in a regulatory or supervisory capacity.
Oil prices: The market value per unit of crude oil, which fluctuates based on global supply and demand factors.
Diesel exports: The volume of diesel fuel shipped from one country to another for international sale and consumption.
Supply risks: Potential disruptions or uncertainties in the availability of a commodity that can influence market pricing.
Passive investing: An investment strategy that aims to maximize returns by minimizing buying and selling, typically by tracking a market index.
Active management: An investment approach where a portfolio manager makes specific investments with the goal of outperforming a market benchmark.
inflation: A general increase in prices and a fall in the purchasing value of money.
midterm elections: General elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term of office.
Reserve Bank of India: The central bank of India responsible for monetary policy and the regulation of the country's currency.
importers: Entities or businesses that bring goods or services into a country from abroad, which often requires purchasing foreign currency.
digital detox: A period of time during which a person refrains from using electronic devices such as smartphones or computers to reduce stress and focus on social interaction.
hub status: The designation of an airport as a primary connection point for international and domestic flights, which is essential for maintaining global connectivity.
phased approach: A construction strategy where a large-scale project is completed in distinct, manageable stages rather than all at once to control costs and timelines.
connectivity: The extent to which an airport provides access to a wide range of destinations, facilitating trade, tourism, and economic exchange.
third-country deportations: The practice of removing non-citizens from the U.S. to a nation other than their country of origin or citizenship.
due process: The constitutional right to a fair legal hearing before the government can deprive an individual of life, liberty, or property.
bilateral memorandum of understanding: A formal agreement between two parties that outlines the terms and responsibilities of a cooperative arrangement.
order backlog: The total number of aircraft that have been ordered by airlines but have not yet been manufactured or delivered.
fleet: The total collection of aircraft operated by an airline or the global aviation industry.
supply chain: The network of suppliers, manufacturers, and logistics providers involved in producing and delivering aircraft components and engines.
shares: Units of ownership in a corporation that represent a claim on part of the company's assets and earnings.
sales: The total amount of money a company receives from the sale of goods or services during a specific period.
Riemann hypothesis: A famous unsolved mathematical conjecture concerning the distribution of prime numbers.
prime numbers: Natural numbers greater than 1 that have no positive divisors other than 1 and themselves.
integrity checks: Processes or audits designed to verify the accuracy, honesty, and reliability of scientific data and research findings.
raw data: The original, unprocessed information collected during a research study before any analysis or interpretation has been applied.
Decentralized AI: An artificial intelligence architecture where data processing and model training are distributed across a network of independent devices rather than a central server.
Energy use: The total amount of electricity consumed by computing hardware to perform specific AI-related tasks or maintain network operations.
climatologist: A scientist who studies the long-term patterns and trends of the Earth's climate.
remuneration: The total compensation, including salary and benefits, provided to an individual for their work.
Bank Secrecy Act: A US law requiring financial institutions to assist government agencies in detecting and preventing money laundering.
anti-money laundering: Regulations and procedures designed to prevent criminals from disguising illegally obtained funds as legitimate income.
due diligence: The investigation or audit of a potential investment or account to confirm all material facts and compliance requirements.
Macroeconomic: The branch of economics concerned with large-scale or general economic factors, such as interest rates and national productivity.
Microeconomic: The study of how individual households and firms make decisions to allocate limited resources.
Monetary policy: The process by which a central bank manages the money supply and interest rates to influence the economy.
refineries: Industrial facilities where crude oil is transformed and refined into products such as diesel and gasoline.
model weights: Numerical parameters within an AI model that determine how it processes data and generates outputs.
source code: The fundamental set of instructions and programming language written by developers to create software applications.
encrypted: Data that has been encoded so that only authorized parties can access or read the information.
Jeddah flight information region: A specific airspace volume where air traffic services are provided and safety warnings are currently enforced.
Houthi: A militant group identified in the text as responsible for repeated attacks on Saudi aviation infrastructure.
satellite navigation signals: Electronic signals used for aircraft positioning that are currently experiencing interference in the region.
extradition: The legal process by which one jurisdiction delivers a person accused of a crime to another jurisdiction for trial.
jurisdiction: The official power and authority of a court to make legal decisions and judgments over a specific case.
indictment: A formal charge or accusation of a serious crime issued by a prosecutor.
lung adenocarcinoma: A type of non-small cell lung cancer that begins in the mucus-secreting glands of the lung.
radical: In a surgical context, a procedure intended to remove all affected tissue to ensure the complete elimination of a disease.
nodule: A small, distinct mass of tissue or growth that may be benign or malignant.
Six Flags: An amusement park company that operates multiple theme parks across various locations.
satellite internet: A method of providing high-speed internet access via a network of satellites orbiting the Earth.
regulatory approval: The formal permission granted by a government body for a company to conduct specific business activities.
Franchisor: A company that grants the rights to use its brand and business model to independent operators in exchange for fees.
Corporate guarantee: A legal promise where a parent company agrees to cover the financial obligations, such as rent, of its franchisees.
Unsecured claims: Debts or obligations that are not backed by any physical collateral or assets.
hijacking: The act of illegally seizing an aircraft while it is in flight or on the ground.
transponder code: A four-digit code entered into an aircraft's transponder to communicate specific emergency or operational statuses to air traffic control.
trade deal: A formal agreement between countries to reduce barriers to imports and exports.
A company operating in the aerospace sector that is currently seeking a significant loan.
Asian banks: Financial institutions based in Asia that are providing capital to borrowers in the Middle East.
food security: A state where all people have reliable access to a sufficient quantity of affordable, nutritious food.
contract drug-manufacturing: A business model where a company provides manufacturing services to pharmaceutical firms to produce their drug products.
midterm ambitions: The specific financial or operational goals a company aims to achieve over a medium-term period.
shareholders: Individuals or institutions that legally own one or more shares of stock in a public or private corporation.
merger: A business agreement that unites two existing companies into a single new legal entity.
hedging: A risk management strategy used to offset potential losses in an investment by taking an opposite position in a related asset.
government bond: A debt security issued by a national government to support government spending and obligations, typically paying periodic interest.
selloff: A rapid or significant decline in the price of an asset or market due to a high volume of selling.
FDA: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a federal agency responsible for protecting public health by ensuring the safety and efficacy of medical devices.
Middle East: A geopolitical region often monitored by energy markets due to its significant role in global oil production and potential for supply chain disruptions.
Commodity: A raw material or primary agricultural product that can be bought and sold, such as copper or oil.
Australian Securities Exchange: The primary stock exchange in Australia where companies list their shares for public trading.
Low Altitude Economy: An economic sector focused on the commercial use of airspace at lower altitudes, typically involving drones and eVTOL aircraft.
Type Certification: A formal verification process by aviation authorities to ensure an aircraft design meets all applicable airworthiness and safety requirements.
Advanced Air Mobility: An emerging aviation ecosystem that uses highly automated, electric aircraft to transport passengers and cargo in urban and regional environments.
SpaceX: An aerospace company owned by Elon Musk that operates the Starlink satellite network.
certification delays: The postponement of regulatory approval required for new aircraft models to enter commercial service.
ASML: A company that supplies specialized machinery used in the manufacturing of semiconductor chips.
data centers: Facilities that house large amounts of computer systems and associated components to support data processing and storage.
financial guidance: Projections or estimates provided by a company regarding its future financial performance, such as revenue or earnings.
Anti-money laundering: A set of procedures and laws designed to prevent criminals from disguising illegally obtained funds as legitimate income.
Sanctions: Commercial and financial penalties applied by one or more countries against a targeted self-governing state, group, or individual.
Due diligence: The investigation or audit of a potential investment or business transaction to confirm all material facts.
macroeconomic: Relating to the branch of economics concerned with large-scale or general economic factors, such as interest rates and national productivity.
microeconomic: Relating to the branch of economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources.
forward-looking: A decision-making approach that incorporates expectations about future conditions rather than relying solely on current data.
Model weights: The numerical parameters within an AI model that are learned during training and determine its predictive capabilities.
Source code: The fundamental programming instructions that define how a software application functions.
Encrypted: Data that has been encoded so that only authorized parties can access or read the information.
Flight information region: An airspace of defined dimensions within which flight information service and alerting service are provided.
Corporate guarantees: A legal promise where a parent company agrees to cover the financial obligations, such as rent, if a franchisee defaults.
transponder: An electronic device on an aircraft that transmits a signal to ground stations to identify the plane and its status.
Food security: A state where all people have reliable access to a sufficient quantity of affordable, nutritious food.
divest: The process of selling off subsidiary assets, investments, or business units.
gold mining: The process of extracting gold or gold-bearing ore from the ground.
asset manager: A firm that invests pooled funds from clients into securities to achieve specific investment goals.
share price: The current market value of a single unit of ownership in a corporation.
Shares: Units of ownership interest in a corporation or financial asset that provide for an equal distribution in any profits.
menu: A list of food and beverage offerings available for purchase at a restaurant.
consumer: An individual who purchases goods or services for personal use.
artificial intelligence: A field of computer science dedicated to creating systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence.
Data centers: Facilities that house large groups of networked computer servers used for the remote storage, processing, or distribution of data.
Semiconductor: A material, often silicon, used to create the electronic chips that power modern computing and artificial intelligence.
scientific integrity: The adherence to ethical principles and professional standards in the performance and reporting of scientific research.
AI-enabled: Systems or processes that utilize artificial intelligence to enhance capabilities or automate complex tasks.
Satellite navigation: A system that uses satellites to provide autonomous geo-spatial positioning, which can be subject to interference in conflict zones.
thoracic: Relating to the thorax, or the part of the body between the neck and the abdomen, including the lungs.
Extradition: The formal process by which one state surrenders an individual to another state for prosecution or punishment for crimes.
Sabotage: The deliberate act of damaging or destroying infrastructure or equipment to hinder an enemy or opponent.
Jurisdiction: The official power or authority of a court to make legal decisions and judgments over a specific case.
Market analysis: The process of evaluating the factors that influence the price and performance of financial assets within a specific sector or region.
Saudi Aramco: The state-owned oil company of Saudi Arabia and one of the world's largest energy producers.
liquefied natural gas: Natural gas that has been cooled to a liquid state for easier storage and transport.
trading house: A diversified company that engages in the import and export of a wide range of goods and commodities.
proprietary research: Information or technology owned by a company that is kept confidential to maintain a competitive advantage.
private equity: Investment funds that buy and restructure companies that are not publicly traded or take public companies private.
FTSE 100: A share index of the 100 companies listed on the London Stock Exchange with the highest market capitalization.
Blue-chip index: A market index composed of shares in large, well-established, and financially sound companies.
semiconductor chips: Electronic components made from materials like silicon that serve as the fundamental building blocks for modern computing and artificial intelligence hardware.
ISA: An Individual Savings Account that allows UK residents to invest or save money without paying tax on interest or capital gains.
Inheritance tax: A tax paid on the estate of someone who has died, which is increasingly impacting pension assets.
FOI request: A formal request made under Freedom of Information legislation to access data held by public authorities like HMRC.
influence peddling: The illegal or unethical practice of using one's government position or personal connections to gain favors or preferential treatment for others.
memecoin: A cryptocurrency that originates from an internet meme or has some other humorous characteristic, often experiencing high volatility.
Domestic Emoluments Clause: A provision in the U.S. Constitution prohibiting the president from receiving additional compensation from the federal government beyond their official salary.
pro bono: Professional work undertaken voluntarily and without payment, often for the public good.
